review_generation.input:
You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

Seawater Mg/Ca has oscillated markedly over the Phanerozoic, closely associated with secular variations in sedimentation, icehouse-greenhouse fluctuations, and the evolution of calcifying invertebrates. However, the drivers of these long-term oscillations remain unresolved. Here, we develop an inverse model that couples seawater Mg concentration and Mg isotope composition variations. By exploiting the contrasting Mg isotopic fractionation associated with Mg-silicate formation and dolomitization, this model quantifies the major marine Mg sinks. Model results show that increases in seawater Mg/Ca during supercontinent assembly were explained by reduced rates of silicate alteration and dolomitization. In contrast, decreases in seawater Mg/Ca during periods of supercontinent stasis and early breakup were driven by intensified Mg-silicate formation and dolomitization. Variations in marine Mg-silicate and dolomite formation were further regulated by seafloor spreading, continental configuration, and climate throughout the supercontinent cycle. Together, our results identify the supercontinent cycle as a first-order regulator of Phanerozoic seawater Mg/Ca through its control on marine Mg-silicate and dolomite fluxes.

---

## Introduction

Seawater chemistry is regulated by a dynamic balance between elemental inputs and outputs via river discharge, hydrothermal fluids, seawater-rock reactions, and the formation of authigenic and biogenic minerals in marine sediments1,2. Magnesium and calcium are the second- and third-most abundant cations in seawater, and proxy data indicate their concentrations have varied considerably over the Phanerozoic, resulting in a maximum seawater Mg/Ca ratio of approximately 5 at present and minima of <1 during the Jurassic–Cretaceous and Cambrian–Carboniferous intervals (Fig. 1a). These periodic changes in seawater Mg/Ca have driven oscillations in the dominant mineralogy of marine carbonates, late-stage evaporites, and invertebrate skeletons throughout the Phanerozoic, and closely coincide with transitions between icehouse and greenhouse climate states (Fig. 1)1. It is well established that riverine input is a major process introducing Mg and Ca into the oceans, while both dolomitization and seafloor alteration remove Mg and add Ca, and the marine Ca budget is additionally regulated by calcium carbonate burial3–7, yet the relative importance of these processes in driving Phanerozoic seawater Mg/Ca variations remains difficult to quantify1,8. The prevailing view attributes seawater Mg/Ca variations to fluctuations in mid-ocean ridge hydrothermal fluxes9 or the rate of dolomitization3,4, since both processes remove Mg and release Ca to seawater, whereas some studies emphasize the role of authigenic clay formation in removing Mg from seawater during the Cenozoic10,11. Uncertainty in the relative contributions of these processes to seawater Mg/Ca arises from the incomplete nature of the geological record, which limits accurate reconstructions of past elemental fluxes1,4,6. Additionally, attributing changes in seawater Mg/Ca to specific processes is challenged by the difficulty in resolving Mg and Ca flux variations associated with individual sources and sinks1.

Integrating the seawater Mg/Ca record with Mg isotopic compositions (δ²⁶Mg, defined as [(²⁶Mg/²⁴Mg)sample / (²⁶Mg/²⁴Mg)standard – 1]×1000, where the standard is DSM3) enables identification of the processes controlling the marine Mg budget, because the formation of Mg-silicates and dolomite in the ocean overall fractionates Mg isotopes in opposite directions12. Consequently, variations in seawater δ²⁶Mg can distinguish between changes in seawater [Mg] driven primarily by Mg-silicate versus dolomite formation and associated geological processes10. This approach has been successfully applied to elucidate mechanisms underpinning seawater Mg/Ca variations during several key geological periods10,11,13,14.

Here, we develop an inverse model of the marine Mg cycle to quantitatively constrain the major processes that have driven seawater Mg/Ca variations throughout the Phanerozoic. By integrating the latest seawater [Mg] and δ²⁶Mg records into the model and comparing the results with Phanerozoic tectonic and climate reconstructions, we find that rising Mg/Ca ratios during supercontinent assembly result from reduced rates of silicate alteration and dolomitization, whereas declining ratios during breakup stem from intensified removal into these sinks. These results demonstrate that the long-term evolution of seawater Mg/Ca is fundamentally regulated by the supercontinent cycle and the associated changes in tectonics and climate.

---

## Results

Inverse model development
Magnesium is a conservative element in seawater with a modern residence time of ca. 12 Myr15. Variations in seawater Mg/Ca are driven by long-term changes in continental weathering-derived riverine input, and by changes in the rates of Mg removal through i) silicate formation via high-temperature (>90 °C) hydrothermal reactions at the mid-ocean ridges (HT), ii) silicate formation via low-temperature (<90 °C) processes including seafloor alteration on ridge flanks and clay authigenesis (LT), and iii) dolomitization (dol)1,8. According to mass balance, the oceanic Mg inventory (N) and Mg isotopic composition (δSW) at a given time (t+Δt) are determined by the seawater Mg budget and δ²⁶Mg at time t, and the cumulative effects of sources and sinks over this period:

N(t+Δt) = N(t) + Δt [Friv(t) - FHT(t) - FLT(t) - Fdol(t)] (1)

N(t+Δt) δSW(t+Δt) = N(t) δSW(t) + Δt [Friv(t) δriv(t) - FHT(t) (δSW(t) + ΔHT-SW) - FLT(t) (δSW(t) + ΔLT-SW) - Fdol(t) (δSW(t) + Δdol-SW)] (2)

By applying these mass-balance equations, we can quantify the fluxes of Mg sources and sinks over the Phanerozoic, since key parameters are well constrained and their uncertainties can be robustly propagated. Seawater [Mg] and δ²⁶Mg are known throughout the Phanerozoic (Fig. 1), and N can be calculated using seawater [Mg] and assuming a constant Phanerozoic seawater mass of 1.4 × 10²¹ kg15. The Mg sinks associated with the formation of Mg-silicate and dolomite have known fractionation factors (Supplementary Table 1). For Mg-silicate formation at high temperature, ΔHT-SW is set as 0‰ due to the quantitative removal of Mg from fluid to crust6,16. For low-temperature Mg-silicate formation, including both seafloor alteration and clay authigenesis, we assign a ΔLT-SW of 0.8 ± 0.2‰ to cover a wider range of previous constraints based on marine clays, altered crust, and hydrothermal fluids5,17–19. For dolomitization, Δdol-SW has been experimentally constrained20: Δdol-SW = -0.1554(±0.0096) × 10⁶/T², with a calculated Δdol-SW of -1.8 ± 0.1‰ at 20 °C. We allow Δdol-SW to vary with Phanerozoic temperature21 and propagate the associated uncertainty.

The modern weighted average global riverine δ²⁶Mg (δriv) is -1.09 ± 0.05‰, primarily controlled by the mixture between carbonate and silicate weathering-derived Mg22. In our model, δriv is taken as increasing from -0.9 ± 0.1‰ in the Cambrian to the modern value of -1.09 ± 0.1‰ (Supplementary Fig. 1), following a modest Phanerozoic increase in carbonate weathering13.

To determine the unknown fluxes, riverine Mg input (Friv) and Mg removal via Mg-silicate formation (FHT and FLT) and dolomitization (Fdol), we performed Monte Carlo simulations, sampling across their plausible ranges and retaining combinations that reproduce the observed seawater [Mg] and δ²⁶Mg records. For each 1-Ma time step backwards from 0 to 550 Ma, 1,000,000 random parameter sets were generated within ranges of 4.5–6 Tmol/yr for Friv, 1–3 Tmol/yr for FHT, 0.6–2.5 Tmol/yr for FLT, and 1–4 Tmol/yr for Fdol that cover previous estimates (see Methods and Supplementary Table 2 for reference). At each time step, we computed the predicted N and δSW using Eqs. (1–2), and retained only those simulated parameter sets whose outputs matched the observed records within a relative 1% tolerance (accepted number > 20,000 per step). All Monte Carlo simulations and data analyses were performed in R (v4.3.1), and the code is provided in the Code Availability section. Uncertainties in accepted solutions for each flux are shown as 68% and 95% confidence intervals in Fig. 2. Since modeled FHT and FLT are nearly identical at each step and highly correlated over the Phanerozoic (R² = 0.84; Supplementary Figs. 2−3), they are combined as a total Mg-silicate sink (Fsil; Fig. 2c) in subsequent discussions.

Our inverse model avoids reliance on fragmentary sedimentary records or uncertain tectonic reconstructions and enables the simultaneous quantification of the major Mg fluxes into and out of ocean water over the Phanerozoic. Moreover, by including the variation of seawater [Mg] in Eq. (1), our model explicitly incorporates temporal variations in Mg residence time. To test the robustness of our results, we performed local sensitivity tests in which each input variable was varied within its data-driven uncertainty and the resulting ensembles were evaluated using Partial Rank Correlation Coefficients (PRCC) and local Δrange effect sizes to quantify short-term, monotonic controls on each flux. These local tests capture how small, realistic deviations in seawater [Mg], δ²⁶MgSW, Δdol-SW, ΔLT-SW, δ²⁶Mgriv, and prior input ranges propagate into Friv, Fdol, and Fsil at each time step (see Methods for details). For the secular analysis, we first calculated time-step mean fluxes and then aggregated them into 20-Myr bins, relating the binned mean fluxes to the slowly varying boundary conditions, including seawater [Mg], δ²⁶MgSW, Δdol-SW, and δ²⁶Mgriv, using a Deming regression that accounts for uncertainties in both variables.

Our sensitivity tests show that, for the integrated time step flux variations, the directions of flux changes are primarily governed by δ²⁶MgSW whereas their magnitudes are mainly controlled by seawater [Mg], with the prescribed Friv range additionally modulating its own variability (Fig. 3; Supplementary Figs. 4–9). Over the whole Phanerozoic, δ²⁶MgSW continues to dictate the direction of dolomite and riverine flux, while seawater [Mg] mainly determines the direction of Fsil. Variations in dolomite and riverine fluxes are mainly controlled by δ²⁶MgSW, while Fsil variation is dominated by seawater [Mg] (Fig. 4). We additionally explored scenarios in which the FLT is higher than the FHT (FLT = 1–3 Tmol/yr and FHT = 0.6–2.5 Tmol/yr). The resulting solutions are indistinguishable from our primary outputs (Supplementary Fig. 10), demonstrating that the assumption of a higher FHT relative to FLT does not influence our results. Together, these analyses demonstrate that the inferred controls on all Mg fluxes arise predominantly from the intrinsic mass-balance framework and from seawater [Mg] and δ²⁶MgSW variations, rather than from prior ranges of input-flux or isotope-fractionation factors.

Major drivers of phanerozoic seawater Mg/Ca variation
The Phanerozoic evolution of seawater [Mg] can be divided into six stages according to our fitted curve, comprising two full cycles of decreasing, fluctuating (minor variation), and increasing seawater [Mg] (Fig. 2a). Seawater [Mg] decreased from 550 to 500 Ma, remained relatively stable with minor fluctuations between 500 and 390 Ma, and increased from 390 to 310 Ma. The second cycle began with a decline in seawater [Mg] from 310 to 200 Ma, followed by a fluctuating interval between 200 and 90 Ma, and a final increase from 90 to 0 Ma. These intervals closely parallel secular variations in seawater Mg/Ca and the timing of aragonite–calcite transitions (Fig. 2a). In our model, we force source-sink net Mg imbalance (Fluxsource-sink) to co-vary with seawater [Mg] to maintain mass balance, ensuring positive Fluxsource-sink values during seawater [Mg] increase periods (Fig. 2e). Over the Phanerozoic, average Mg flux ranges are 5.2–5.4 Tmol/yr for Friv, 1.4–2.8 Tmol/yr for Fdol, and 2.9–3.9 Tmol/yr for Fsil (Fig. 2b–e).

Seawater [Mg] varies in concert with seawater Mg/Ca throughout the Phanerozoic, and the same geological drivers that regulate seawater [Mg] also control seawater Mg/Ca. Seawater [Mg] and [Ca] are independently reconstructed by measuring Mg and Ca concentrations of fluid inclusions in early-stage primary marine halite23, and their inverse evolution, together with the co-variation of seawater [Mg] and Mg/Ca (Fig. 1a–b), suggests that these secular variations are driven by the same geological processes. During intervals of decreasing and increasing seawater [Mg], seawater [Mg] and Mg/Ca show strong positive correlations (R² = 0.93–0.99; Supplementary Fig. 11), indicating that processes responsible for [Mg] changes also regulate Ca and the Mg/Ca ratio. This is reasonable since two major geological processes, seafloor alteration and dolomitization, involve 1:1 Mg-Ca exchange, such that seawater [Mg] increases correspond to [Ca] decreases and vice versa. In contrast, during intervals of minor seawater [Mg] fluctuations, correlations between [Mg] and Mg/Ca weaken (R² = 0.01–0.53; Supplementary Fig. 11) while seawater [Ca] varied significantly (Fig. 1b). This indicates that independent Ca-related processes, such as calcium carbonate burial, also considerably regulate seawater Mg/Ca during these periods. For instance, the development of pelagic calcification since the Mesozoic may have significantly contributed to declining seawater [Ca]24. In the following sections, we focus on the primary controls on major seawater Mg/Ca transitions between aragonite and calcite seas, while secondary fluctuations within prolonged calcite-sea intervals (ca. 500–390 and 200–90 Ma) may be better constrained through future studies of the marine Ca cycle.

The limited Friv variation in our results does not suggest invariant Friv in the geological record; instead, it reflects the relative insensitivity of Mg mass balance to Friv within plausible ranges. The modest Friv increases during the 420–370 Ma and 50–0 Ma periods coincide with the assembly of the supercontinent Pangea and Alpine-Himalayan collision (Fig. 2b), suggesting enhanced weathering flux during supercontinent assembly. The increase in Friv during 550–500 Ma may reflect intensified weathering and a reorganized clay factory associated with widespread felsic terrains, high continental topography, and elevated CO₂ outgassing14,25–27. However, our model cannot resolve the precise magnitude of these variations. This insensitivity does not substantially affect our interpretation because weathering generally alters Mg and Ca inputs in the same direction unless global lithology changes substantially, and the Phanerozoic continental lithologic composition appears to have remained broadly stable28. Nevertheless, short-lived shifts in lithology can influence riverine Mg/Ca, because calcium carbonate (Mg/Ca ≈ 0.1)4, dolomite (Mg/Ca = 1.0)29, and silicate rocks (Mg/Ca ≈ 0.4 to 0.7)30 contribute distinct Mg/Ca signatures. For instance, the extensive exposure of basalt-mafic rocks during the formation of Pangea at the late Permian31, the enhanced development of carbonate platforms during the breakup of Pangea at the Jurassic-Cretaceous32, and the Alpine-Himalayan Collision during the Cenozoic mountain uplift33 may involve significant changes in global continental lithology. Improved constraints on continental weathering fluxes and lithologic evolution across these intervals would further refine estimates of riverine Mg delivery and Mg/Ca modulation.

Finally, Phanerozoic seawater Mg/Ca variations can be primarily attributed to substantial changes in dolomite and Mg-silicate fluxes. Between 550 and 500 Ma, intense Mg-silicate removal coincided with net Mg loss (e.g., negative Fluxsource-sink), leading to a decline in seawater Mg/Ca, while subsequent weakening of this sink mitigated this decline; the dolomite sink remained nearly constant (Fig. 2). From 500 to 390 Ma, a slight decrease in Fdol combined with an initial rise and subsequent fall in Fsil yielded slightly positive and later negative Fluxsource-sink, accounting for fluctuating seawater Mg/Ca within this prolonged calcite sea period (Fig. 2a–d). Between 390 and 310 Ma, rising seawater Mg/Ca was first driven by a sharp reduction in the dolomite sink (390–340 Ma), followed by weakening of the Mg-silicate sink at 340–310 Ma (Fig. 2a–d). From 310 to 200 Ma, concurrent peaks in both dolomite and Mg-silicate fluxes caused renewed Mg removal and a further decline in Mg/Ca. Despite decreases in both sinks after 240 Ma, Fluxsource-sink remained negative, sustaining the downward trend (Fig. 2a–d). During 200–90 Ma, reduced dolomitization was offset by enhanced Mg-silicate removal, maintaining fluctuating seawater Mg/Ca (Fig. 2a–d). Since 90 Ma, rising seawater [Mg] was driven by a persistent decline in the dolomite sink, amplified after 40 Ma by weakening Mg-silicate removal (Fig. 2a–d).

Controls on Mg-silicate and dolomite fluxes
Marine Mg-silicate formation is considered to be dominated by seawater–seafloor reactions, with clay authigenesis contributing negligibly under Phanerozoic conditions of low dissolved silica and cooler bottom-water temperatures34. For instance, the modern ocean hosts an authigenic clay sink of only 0.02 Tmol/yr5, representing ~0.6% of the total Mg-silicate sink. Mg-silicate flux during seafloor alteration is mainly controlled by seafloor spreading, with faster spreading rates producing more fresh ocean crust available for hydrothermal alteration and Mg-silicate formation7. The tight correlation between FHT and FLT further supports a dominant driver of seafloor spreading on both fluxes (Supplementary Figs. 2–3), with the authigenic clay sink playing only a minor role.

Mg-silicate flux exhibits five prominent peaks at ca. 550, 420, 335, 240, and 110–40 Ma (Fig. 2c). Four of five peaks lag the corresponding maxima in reconstructed global seafloor production rate by 10–30 Myr, consistent with the observation that most hydrothermal alteration of oceanic crust occurs within 30 Myr of crustal accretion6,35. The exception at ca. 420 Ma, which lags the production maximum by ~50 Myr (Fig. 2c), may reflect uncertainties in fluid-inclusion [Mg] data and/or prolonged seafloor–seawater reactions, which can persist for up to 80 Myr35. Notably, the protracted Mg-silicate flux between ~140 and 40 Ma closely matches previously reconstructed hydrothermal fluxes during Pangea dispersal (140–35 Ma; Fig. 2f–g)36. Moreover, Fsil is negatively correlated with the continental fragmentation index during Pangea early assembly (500–320 Ma) and positively correlated during dispersal (200–0 Ma; Fig. 2c, g; Supplementary Fig. 12). These relationships indicate that Mg-silicate formation was significantly enhanced during active tectonic phases (assembly and breakup), whereas it was attenuated during periods of supercontinent stasis. These relationships highlight a strong coupling between the supercontinent cycle, seafloor production, and marine Mg-silicate formation.

Controls on dolomitization rate remain unclear. High sea level29, warm climates13,37, large-scale restriction38, the dissolution-reprecipitation process39, oceanic anoxia40, and microbial activity41 have all been proposed to promote dolomite formation. Microbial activity, elevated temperatures, and restricted hydrological conditions are suggested to accelerate dolomite nucleation and crystal growth37,39,41, while anoxic conditions can further stimulate microbial metabolisms that catalyze dolomitization. High sea level promotes expansive shallow platforms and accelerates reaction kinetics through enhanced evaporation and elevated temperatures, particularly in warm, semi-restricted settings29. Sea level and climate are fundamentally modulated by tectonics: supercontinent assembly leads to a lower sea level due to thermal contraction of aging seafloor and crustal thickening during continental collision, whereas breakup creates younger seafloor and thinner crust, raising sea level42,43. Warm climates typically accompany early supercontinent breakup, when diminished continental collision reduces silicate weathering, and increased arc volcanism, mantle plumes, and large igneous provinces drive rapid pCO₂ increases26,44,45. Large-scale restriction is controlled by global tectonic configuration46, while oceanic anoxia and microbial activity are influenced by atmospheric O₂ and broader environmental conditions, which have also been linked to the supercontinent cycle47,48.

Dolomite abundance has been reconstructed using various approaches, providing an independent benchmark for comparison with our dolomite flux evolution. Our modeled dolomite flux reproduces the major features of sedimentary records, including high dolomite abundance in the early Paleozoic and across the Permian–Triassic boundary, reduced values during the Mississippian, and a long-term decline since the early Mesozoic (Fig. 2d, 5)29,40. We further standardized all dolomite abundance curves through age alignment and long-term trend extraction using Generalized Additive Models and Locally Estimated Scatterplot Smoothing, to directly compare dolomite flux with those dolomite abundance curves. Spearman’s rank correlations (ρ) and bootstrap resampling of the aligned trends show strong agreement between our dolomite flux and three of the five sedimentary records (Fig. 5, Supplementary Fig. 13; ρ > 0.67). The remaining two records show weaker agreement due to intrinsic limitations, one with extremely low temporal resolution, and the other exhibiting a temporal pattern distinct from the broader dataset (Fig. 5).

Correlations between dolomite flux and environmental factors suggest that the dominant controls on dolomitization varied over the Phanerozoic. Dolomite flux is generally high in the early Paleozoic and declines through the Mesozoic, mirroring the secular evolution of atmospheric pO₂ (Fig. 5), suggesting a potential role of oceanic anoxia and microbial mediation on secular dolomite formation. Moreover, dolomite flux shows strong positive correlations with modeled pCO₂ (550–340 and 250–0 Ma) and reconstructed sea level (460–340 and 100–0 Ma) during most Phanerozoic intervals (Fig. 5, Supplementary Fig. 11), consistent with dominant control of climatic and eustatic variations on dolomite formation. However, the pronounced rise in dolomite flux between 340 and 250 Ma coincides with a low pCO₂ and low sea level interval (Fig. 5), suggesting other factors also influence dolomitization. This elevated dolomite flux may be attributed to the restriction of the Paleotethys Ocean during Pangea assembly38, which is also favored by arid continental climates and widespread evaporite deposition46 during this period.

The role of Phanerozoic supercontinent cycles on seawater Mg/Ca
Previous studies have emphasized the influence of tectonics and climate on Phanerozoic seawater Mg/Ca8,36,49, yet direct constraints on how these processes modulated marine Mg fluxes have been lacking. Our model quantitatively constrains variations in Mg-silicate and dolomite fluxes and reveals their tight links to specific tectonic–climatic processes (Fig. 2). Across the Phanerozoic, high Mg/Ca ratios broadly coincide with low sea level and coolhouse conditions associated with supercontinent assembly and major collisional phases, whereas low Mg/Ca ratios correspond to high sea level and greenhouse climates during supercontinent dispersal (Fig. 2). Our results show that this inverse relationship between seawater Mg/Ca and sea level reflects the combined impact of tectonics and climate on Mg-silicate formation and dolomitization. Collectively, these findings imply that the supercontinent cycle exerted a first-order control on Phanerozoic seawater Mg/Ca.

The supercontinent cycle regulates Phanerozoic seawater Mg/Ca as follows: during supercontinent early assembly (e.g. Pangea) or major collisional events (e.g. Cenozoic Alpine-Himalayan collisions), attenuated seafloor spreading and cooler climates suppress Mg-silicate formation and dolomitization, thereby increasing seawater Mg/Ca and shifting global oceans from calcite to aragonite seas (Fig. 6a). During periods of supercontinent early breakup, enhanced seafloor spreading and warmer climates stimulate both Mg-silicate formation and dolomitization, lowering Mg/Ca and returning the oceans to calcite seas (Fig. 6b). During intervals of stable supercontinent dispersal or sluggish plate reorganization, both tectonic and climatic conditions remain relatively steady, yielding limited variability in Mg fluxes and sustaining prolonged calcite seas (Fig. 6c). The supercontinent cycle also drives long-term variations in calcium carbonate deposition by modulating global shelf area50. Supercontinent breakup expands flooded margins and enhances CaCO₃ burial, whereas assembly contracts shelf space and suppresses CaCO₃ deposition. Because this process consumes more Ca during breakup and dispersal but significantly less during assembly, and contributes only marginally to the marine Mg cycle, its influence on Phanerozoic seawater Mg/Ca is likely important only during seawater [Mg] fluctuation periods (Fig. 2a).

Beyond Mg/Ca, the supercontinent cycle has been invoked to regulate other major and trace elements in seawater. Phanerozoic seawater sulfate shows a broadly similar evolution to Mg, which potentially reflects enhanced removal during high-sea-level intervals when microbial sulfate reduction8 and Ca-driven sulfate precipitation intensified49. Seawater Sr and Li concentrations also appear tied to the supercontinent cycle, decreasing during assembly and rising during breakup and dispersal, likely due to their sensitivity to changes in hydrothermal fluid fluxes51,52. These trace elements, strongly modulated by hydrothermal activity51,52, are therefore particularly responsive to tectonic reorganization associated with supercontinent cycling.

By integrating elemental and isotopic records into a marine Mg-cycle model, our study provides quantitative estimates of long-term fluxes through the major Mg sinks in seawater. This advance allows seawater Mg/Ca variability to be more directly attributed to specific geological processes. Our results offer a framework for interpreting Phanerozoic seawater chemistry variations and demonstrate that these variations reflect coupled interactions among ocean chemistry, sedimentation, climate, and the supercontinent cycle.

---

## Methods

Model inputs
Required parameters in our model include Δdol-SW, ΔHT-SW, ΔLT-SW, and input ranges of Friv, FHT, FLT, and Fdol. Temperature-dependent Δdol-SW has been experimentally constrained20: Δdol-SW = -0.1554(±0.0096) × 10⁶/T². Calculated Δdol-SW is -1.8 ± 0.1‰ at 20 °C. Considering the variation of Earth’s surface temperature from ~9 to ~33 °C in the Phanerozoic21, we allow Δdol-SW to vary with temperature and propagate uncertainty in the equation (from -1.95 ± 0.1‰ to -1.66 ± 0.1‰). During high-temperature seafloor-seawater reactions, Mg is removed quantitatively from fluid to crust with nil isotope fractionation6,16, and we therefore set ΔHT-SW to 0‰. During low-temperature Mg-silicate formation, previous studies consistently suggest a positive ΔLT-SW, varying from 0.1‰ to 1.1‰ in authigenic clays5, with average values of 0.8‰ to 1‰ in altered oceanic crust17,18, and 0.25‰ to 7‰ in hydrothermal fluids19. Most studies adopt 0.6–0.8‰, and we therefore set 0.8 ± 0.2‰ to encompass a relatively large range in previous constraints. Reference ranges of these isotope fractionation in previous studies and this study are summarized in Supplementary Table 1.

Ranges of Friv, FHT, FLT, and Fdol for the implementation of Monte Carlo simulations in our model are grounded in previous estimates on modern and Phanerozoic models. Previous estimates on Friv, FHT, FLT, and Fdol range from 4 to 6.1 Tmol/yr, 0.24 to 2.6 Tmol/yr, 0.6 to 2.5 Tmol/yr, and 0.75 to 3 Tmol/yr, and we set a range of 4.5–6 Tmol/yr, 1–3 Tmol/yr, 0.6–2.5 Tmol/yr, and 1–4 Tmol/yr for input ranges of Friv, FHT, FLT, and Fdol in our model (Supplementary Table 2). Since some studies suggest lower FHT than that of FLT19, we also considered a scenario using ranges of 1–3 Tmol/yr for FLT and 0.6–2.5 Tmol/yr for FHT, which resulted in identical results to our primary outputs (Supplementary Fig. 10). To verify whether these inputs can effectively cover the actual ranges of these fluxes over the whole Phanerozoic and whether these prior input ranges would affect our model outputs, we further included variable upper and lower ranges for these fluxes at each time step to quantify their effect on our results in the following sensitivity tests.

Sensitivity test
We evaluate two types of controls on the modeled riverine, Mg-silicate, and dolomite Mg fluxes: (1) local sensitivity at each individual time step, and (2) secular drivers across the Phanerozoic. The local sensitivity quantifies which parameters constrain flux magnitudes within a given time step, whereas the secular analysis identifies which boundary conditions primarily explain the long-term evolution of these fluxes through Earth’s history. For both analyses, we use Partial Rank Correlation Coefficients (PRCC) to quantify the independent (partial) monotonic control of each variable on each flux, and we use Δrange metrics (ΔY or ΔF) to quantify the corresponding amplitude of that control in physical units (Tmol/yr).

Monte Carlo sampling was used to identify flux combinations satisfying mass–isotope balance, whereas Latin Hypercube Sampling was employed to systematically explore parameter sensitivities around these solutions. For each time step, we generated 3×10⁴ Latin Hypercube samples (LHS) covering the full range of model parameters. LHS provides uniform, stratified coverage of the parameter space, enabling efficient yet comprehensive exploration of model behavior. Local perturbations follow the data-driven uncertainties: seawater [Mg] is drawn from 68% confidence bounds, and δ²⁶MgSW is perturbed by ± 0.2‰, which is derived from current uncertainty in the reconstructed Phanerozoic curve13. Δdol–SW is drawn via the temperature-dependent coefficient (0.1554 ± 0.0096) × 10⁶/T², ΔLT–SW is sampled in 0.6–1.0‰, and δ²⁶Mgriv in ± 0.1‰. Physically plausible Mg fluxes are allowed by first drawing a lower and upper bound for each flux in Tmol/yr, then sampling uniformly within that interval: Friv is allowed to vary between ~4.5 and 6.0 Tmol/yr (Friv_min = 4.5–5.0; Friv_max = 5.5–6.0), Fdol between ~1 and 4 Tmol/yr (Fdol_min = 1.0–1.5; Fdol_max = 3.5–4.0), FHT between 1 and 3 Tmol/yr (FHT_min = 1.0–1.5; FHT_max = 2.5–3.0), and FLT between 0.6 and 2.5 Tmol/yr (FLT_min = 0.6–1.2; FLT_max = 2.0–2.5). These accepted ensembles form the foundation for both the local and secular analyses, while parameters that exhibit genuine secular trends are evaluated in the secular framework. Local sensitivity therefore reflects uncertainty within each geological interval, whereas the secular analysis evaluates the effect of boundary-condition evolution through time.

(a) Partial Rank Correlation Coefficients (PRCC)
PRCC quantifies the monotonic influence of each parameter (Xᵢ) on a modeled flux (Y) while removing covariation with all other parameters. For the local analysis, at each time step, all variables are rank-transformed, Xᵢ and Y are separately regressed against all remaining parameters, and the Spearman correlation (ρ) between their residuals defines the local PRCC:

PRCC(Xᵢ, Y) = ρ(rXi, rY) (3)

The sign indicates whether Xᵢ increases or decreases Y, and |PRCC| measures the strength of that relationship. |PRCC| values are interpreted following common practice, with higher absolute values indicating stronger monotonic influence. Local PRCCs reveal, for each time step, which parameters co-vary with the flux to satisfy Mg mass–isotope balance. For each time step, we additionally apply a nonparametric bootstrap by resampling the accepted Monte Carlo ensembles with replacement (1000 iterations) and recalculating PRCC, yielding a bootstrap distribution for that interval. The bootstrap median provides a stable PRCC estimate for that specific time step. We then integrate all local PRCC results across ~550 time steps to compute the median and interquartile range (IQR) for each parameter–flux pair.

(b) Effect size (Δrange).
To complement the correlation-based PRCC, we compute the physical amplitude of each parameter’s effect using Δrange metrics. In the local analysis, all accepted ensembles within a given time step are sorted by parameter X and divided into quantile bins; the difference between median fluxes in the highest and lowest bins define the local effect size (ΔY):

ΔY = median(Y|Xhigh) - median(Y|Xlow) (4)

ΔY (in Tmol/yr) represents the characteristic amplitude by which that parameter can shift the flux within that specific interval. Within each time step, ΔY is also bootstrapped by resampling accepted ensembles and recalculating ΔY 1000 times, producing a bootstrap ΔY distribution whose median represents the interval-specific effect size. Local ΔY values are likewise summarized across ~550 time steps (median ± IQR), where the reported 550 Ma statistics are derived from the set of per-interval bootstrap medians, reflecting long-term variability in effect magnitude.

(c) Secular drivers (20 Myr binned Deming regression with bootstrap)
To evaluate the leverage of boundary conditions on long-term flux evolution over the Phanerozoic, time-series data were aggregated into 20 Myr bins, and binned mean fluxes (F: Friv, Fsil, Fdol) were related to binned boundary conditions (X: seawater [Mg], δ²⁶MgSW, δ²⁶Mgriv, Δdol–SW). We first applied a Deming (total least-squares) regression, which accounts for uncertainties in both X and F, to estimate the secular slope:

F = a + bX, b = dF/dX (5)

ΔF = b × (Xmax - Xmin) (6)

Where b is the long-term Deming slope (dF/dX), ΔF is the flux change implied by the secular range of X, and the coefficient of determination (R²) is computed from fitted versus observed fluxes to evaluate explanatory power. The secular analysis is limited to parameters that exhibit genuine secular trends and can therefore drive multi-million-year flux evolution, whereas time-invariant parameters such as ΔLT-SW or prior ranges only affect local solutions and are not evaluated in the secular framework. We then apply a nonparametric bootstrap that resamples the 20 Myr bins with replacement (N≈27 per iteration), recalculating the Deming slope and ΔF for each realization. The resulting bootstrap medians and IQRs quantify the robustness of long-term relationships to temporal sampling.

The combined framework thus links instantaneous and long-term controls: local PRCC and ΔY capture short-term parameter sensitivity within each interval, their time-integrated medians reveal persistent controls across the Phanerozoic, and the secular regression (ΔF and R²) quantifies the actual magnitude and explanatory power of slow boundary-condition variations.

Building on previous work on the role of supercontinent cycles in regulating seawater chemistry, Zhang et al. combine newly published data on Phanerozoic seawater magnesium concentrations and Mg isotopes, and apply an inverse model to further constrain the sources and sinks of seawater Mg fluxes. Overall, the manuscript contributes to advancing our understanding of the elemental evolution of ancient seawater and its driving mechanisms. However, my main concerns are that (1) the study interprets changes in the Phanerozoic seawater Mg/Ca ratio solely in terms of Mg fluxes, and (2) the correlation between supercontinent cycles and Mg flux does not appear to be particularly strong. I therefore recommend that the manuscript undergo major revision. My specific comments are as follows:

### Reviewer 2

Zhang et al. developed a Mg isotope based inverse model to constrain changes in Mg fluxes of rivers, marine Mg-silicate formation, and dolomitization in the Phanerozoic oceans. Based on their modeling results, they argue that the Phanerozoic marine Mg cycle, including seawater Mg contents and Mg/Ca ratios, has been affected by supercontinent cycles as the first-order control.
This is an interesting study, and the novelty of the research lies in the fact that these authors used the existing Mg records (Mg/Ca, [Mg], and δ26Mg) to deconvolve possible changes in major Mg source (rivers) and sink (Mg-silicates and dolomites) fluxes over the entire Phanerozoic. Although their main conclusion that major ion chemistry of past seawater has been controlled by the tectonic forcing (i.e., supercontinent cycles) is not entirely new, the model-reconstructed Mg fluxes of rivers, Mg-silicates, and dolomites are valuable and significant, if true. This study is of broad interest and suitable for Nature Communications.
The main concern I have for this study is that this manuscript does not provide sufficient validation for their model-generated flux estimates. The principle of the kind of isotope mass balance model developed in this study is well known in literature. At face value, this kind of model can refine elemental source and sink fluxes based on combined elemental and isotopic mass balance equations. However, these refined elemental flux estimates depend on how well end-member Mg isotope compositions (or the relevant Mg isotope fractionation factors) are constrained, as well as how confident we think the previous estimates cover the “true” values of these fluxes. Although these authors presented sensitivity test results, it is challenging to assess if the tested parameter space indeed has covered what is possible in nature. This is particularly true for Mg isotope fractionation factors and how they may have varied over space and time. When it comes to their results, it is surprising to see that riverine Mg flux has remained almost constant over the entire Phanerozoic. If this is true, does it mean the riverine flux has been almost constant for other major ions? I am not suggesting the result to be false, but it is certainly counterintuitive, given that weathering must have varied considerably during the Phanerozoic. I think independent evidence to back up the modelled fluxes is essential but inadequate in the current manuscript.

### Reviewer 3

In this paper, Zhang et al. investigate the drivers behind changes in Mg concentrations throughout the Phanerozoic. To do this, they constructed an isotope mass balance model and used the known ranges in size of the key fluxes and their isotopic values in a Monte Carlo ensemble, to try and reproduce an estimated seawater curve of Phanerozoic Mg concentrations ([Mg]) and isotopic values (δ26Mg ), discarding any model runs which did not match the curve +/- a 1% error. From their results they conclude that supercontinent cycles have driven changes in [Mg].
I think the paper shows just how much information about the Earth system can be gleaned from the use of simple isotope mass balance modelling, so in that regard it is a pretty neat piece of work. But, I feel like the work is lacking in detail in some places, meaning that it is difficult to exactly work out (at the moment) how the model has been constructed. The work could also be more comprehensive in its exploration of some of the uncertainties regarding e.g. isotopic values, but also limitations of the modelling etc. I will detail my concerns, grouping them into major comments and then some minor, easily fixable suggestions.
Major comments
When it comes to the results/discussion sections regarding changes to Mg/Ca and their drivers the sole focus is on variations in Mg. However, you need to include what is going on with [Ca] as inferred by either fluid inclusion data or modelling using Ca isotopes because there are some disparities between the timing and relative magnitude of changes between [Mg] and Mg/Ca, but if the input from riverine is largely invariant as suggested by your modelling, then Mg : Ca exchange is going to be 1:1 so then Fig 1ab / Fig 2a needs a bit more discussion, as this then also relates to the timings of the shift between aragonite and calcite seas you mention. This also then relates to the title you have given the paper – really it only focuses on [Mg] at the moment, barely scratching the surface of [Ca] never mind any other seawater chemistry.
I can understand why you combine low temperature (LT) and high temperature (HT) Mg removal via silicate formation for ease, but I’m guessing this means that your Fsil then has the same isotopic fractionation as the LT flux? I’m having to guess here because, unless I’ve completely missed it, this isn’t explicitly stated. But this means that your results might not be correct because if you keep these fluxes separate, a large HT flux with no isotopic fractionation and a smaller LT flux with some isotopic fractionation (and vice versa - e.g. what happens if, contrary to the rest of the studies, the Shalev paper referenced in the supplement is correct and the HT removal flux is lower than LT) is going to be different than if these are combined with a single fractionation value. Plus splitting these out would provide useful insights into whether LT or HT is key in driving Mg cycle changes. In either case, on L80 you say that you use equations 1 and 2 you compute the predicted [Mg] and δ26Mg but obviously this isn’t strictly true because you’re combining LT and HT, so you should write out new equations to illustrate this. It would also be incredibly helpful to have the isotopic values and their ranges used in a table as you have done with the flux sizes in the supplement.
I think that it is important to include on L53 but also in the discussion section that Mg has a long residence time at present. think this is important to note, because the Xia et al. (2024) paper ignores some of the more rapid changes in δ26Mg , saying that this might be due to restricted basin effects because of the long residence time of Mg. However, other than for the Cenozoic and late Devonian - Permian, [Mg] is quite different and fluctuations are going to be driven by changes to residence time and steady state. Just because the residence time is long now doesn't mean it’s always been that long!
I think there also needs to be more discussion regarding the riverine flux of Mg and its possible effect on [Mg] through the Phanerozoic – just because the mean from your model is largely invariant, it does not mean that there can’t be substantial variations per timestep between the bounds of the confidence intervals, which roughly matches (in terms of Tmol/yr) the size of the variations between the confidence interval bounds for the dolomite flux.

(2024) comes from, albeit I’ve had to just skim through the paper, but there is surely some uncertainty attached to that too. This doesn’t necessarily need modelling, but it needs to be considered when deciding on what range to use for δ26Mg and for your discussion too – how might it affect your results? Bluth and Kump (1991) have paleogeographic maps which can be used to aid some of the discussion.

You previously reviewed this paper and raised several concerns. The authors have now submitted a revised manuscript along with a detailed point-by-point response. Your task is to write your updated review after carefully reading:

  3. The authors' point-by-point response

In your updated review, explicitly state which concerns have been adequately addressed and which remain outstanding. Be specific.

## Paper

## Abstract

Seawater Mg/Ca has oscillated markedly over the Phanerozoic, closely associated with secular variations in sedimentation, icehouse-greenhouse fluctuations, and the evolution of calcifying invertebrates. However, the drivers of these long-term oscillations remain unresolved. Here, we develop an inverse model that couples seawater Mg concentration and Mg isotope composition variations. By exploiting the contrasting Mg isotopic fractionation associated with Mg-silicate formation and dolomitization, this model quantifies the major marine Mg sinks. Model results show that increases in seawater Mg/Ca during supercontinent assembly were explained by reduced rates of silicate alteration and dolomitization. In contrast, decreases in seawater Mg/Ca during periods of supercontinent stasis and early breakup were driven by intensified Mg-silicate formation and dolomitization. Variations in marine Mg-silicate and dolomite formation were further regulated by seafloor spreading, continental configuration, and climate throughout the supercontinent cycle. Together, our results identify the supercontinent cycle as a first-order regulator of Phanerozoic seawater Mg/Ca through its control on marine Mg-silicate and dolomite fluxes.

---

## Introduction

Seawater chemistry is regulated by a dynamic balance between elemental inputs and outputs via river discharge, hydrothermal fluids, seawater-rock reactions, and the formation of authigenic and biogenic minerals in marine sediments1,2. Magnesium and calcium are the second- and third-most abundant cations in seawater, and proxy data indicate their concentrations have varied considerably over the Phanerozoic, resulting in a maximum seawater Mg/Ca ratio of approximately 5 at present and minima of <1 during the Jurassic–Cretaceous and Cambrian–Carboniferous intervals (Fig. 1a). These periodic changes in seawater Mg/Ca have driven oscillations in the dominant mineralogy of marine carbonates, late-stage evaporites, and invertebrate skeletons throughout the Phanerozoic, and closely coincide with transitions between icehouse and greenhouse climate states (Fig. 1)1. It is well established that riverine input is a major process introducing Mg and Ca into the oceans, while both dolomitization and seafloor alteration remove Mg and add Ca, and the marine Ca budget is additionally regulated by calcium carbonate burial3–7, yet the relative importance of these processes in driving Phanerozoic seawater Mg/Ca variations remains difficult to quantify1,8. The prevailing view attributes seawater Mg/Ca variations to fluctuations in mid-ocean ridge hydrothermal fluxes9 or the rate of dolomitization3,4, since both processes remove Mg and release Ca to seawater, whereas some studies emphasize the role of authigenic clay formation in removing Mg from seawater during the Cenozoic10,11. Uncertainty in the relative contributions of these processes to seawater Mg/Ca arises from the incomplete nature of the geological record, which limits accurate reconstructions of past elemental fluxes1,4,6. Additionally, attributing changes in seawater Mg/Ca to specific processes is challenged by the difficulty in resolving Mg and Ca flux variations associated with individual sources and sinks1.

Integrating the seawater Mg/Ca record with Mg isotopic compositions (δ²⁶Mg, defined as [(²⁶Mg/²⁴Mg)sample / (²⁶Mg/²⁴Mg)standard – 1]×1000, where the standard is DSM3) enables identification of the processes controlling the marine Mg budget, because the formation of Mg-silicates and dolomite in the ocean overall fractionates Mg isotopes in opposite directions12. Consequently, variations in seawater δ²⁶Mg can distinguish between changes in seawater [Mg] driven primarily by Mg-silicate versus dolomite formation and associated geological processes10. This approach has been successfully applied to elucidate mechanisms underpinning seawater Mg/Ca variations during several key geological periods10,11,13,14.

Here, we develop an inverse model of the marine Mg cycle to quantitatively constrain the major processes that have driven seawater Mg/Ca variations throughout the Phanerozoic. By integrating the latest seawater [Mg] and δ²⁶Mg records into the model and comparing the results with Phanerozoic tectonic and climate reconstructions, we find that rising Mg/Ca ratios during supercontinent assembly result from reduced rates of silicate alteration and dolomitization, whereas declining ratios during breakup stem from intensified removal into these sinks. These results demonstrate that the long-term evolution of seawater Mg/Ca is fundamentally regulated by the supercontinent cycle and the associated changes in tectonics and climate.

---

## Results

Inverse model development
Magnesium is a conservative element in seawater with a modern residence time of ca. 12 Myr15. Variations in seawater Mg/Ca are driven by long-term changes in continental weathering-derived riverine input, and by changes in the rates of Mg removal through i) silicate formation via high-temperature (>90 °C) hydrothermal reactions at the mid-ocean ridges (HT), ii) silicate formation via low-temperature (<90 °C) processes including seafloor alteration on ridge flanks and clay authigenesis (LT), and iii) dolomitization (dol)1,8. According to mass balance, the oceanic Mg inventory (N) and Mg isotopic composition (δSW) at a given time (t+Δt) are determined by the seawater Mg budget and δ²⁶Mg at time t, and the cumulative effects of sources and sinks over this period:

N(t+Δt) = N(t) + Δt [Friv(t) - FHT(t) - FLT(t) - Fdol(t)] (1)

N(t+Δt) δSW(t+Δt) = N(t) δSW(t) + Δt [Friv(t) δriv(t) - FHT(t) (δSW(t) + ΔHT-SW) - FLT(t) (δSW(t) + ΔLT-SW) - Fdol(t) (δSW(t) + Δdol-SW)] (2)

By applying these mass-balance equations, we can quantify the fluxes of Mg sources and sinks over the Phanerozoic, since key parameters are well constrained and their uncertainties can be robustly propagated. Seawater [Mg] and δ²⁶Mg are known throughout the Phanerozoic (Fig. 1), and N can be calculated using seawater [Mg] and assuming a constant Phanerozoic seawater mass of 1.4 × 10²¹ kg15. The Mg sinks associated with the formation of Mg-silicate and dolomite have known fractionation factors (Supplementary Table 1). For Mg-silicate formation at high temperature, ΔHT-SW is set as 0‰ due to the quantitative removal of Mg from fluid to crust6,16. For low-temperature Mg-silicate formation, including both seafloor alteration and clay authigenesis, we assign a ΔLT-SW of 0.8 ± 0.2‰ to cover a wider range of previous constraints based on marine clays, altered crust, and hydrothermal fluids5,17–19. For dolomitization, Δdol-SW has been experimentally constrained20: Δdol-SW = -0.1554(±0.0096) × 10⁶/T², with a calculated Δdol-SW of -1.8 ± 0.1‰ at 20 °C. We allow Δdol-SW to vary with Phanerozoic temperature21 and propagate the associated uncertainty.

The modern weighted average global riverine δ²⁶Mg (δriv) is -1.09 ± 0.05‰, primarily controlled by the mixture between carbonate and silicate weathering-derived Mg22. In our model, δriv is taken as increasing from -0.9 ± 0.1‰ in the Cambrian to the modern value of -1.09 ± 0.1‰ (Supplementary Fig. 1), following a modest Phanerozoic increase in carbonate weathering13.

To determine the unknown fluxes, riverine Mg input (Friv) and Mg removal via Mg-silicate formation (FHT and FLT) and dolomitization (Fdol), we performed Monte Carlo simulations, sampling across their plausible ranges and retaining combinations that reproduce the observed seawater [Mg] and δ²⁶Mg records. For each 1-Ma time step backwards from 0 to 550 Ma, 1,000,000 random parameter sets were generated within ranges of 4.5–6 Tmol/yr for Friv, 1–3 Tmol/yr for FHT, 0.6–2.5 Tmol/yr for FLT, and 1–4 Tmol/yr for Fdol that cover previous estimates (see Methods and Supplementary Table 2 for reference). At each time step, we computed the predicted N and δSW using Eqs. (1–2), and retained only those simulated parameter sets whose outputs matched the observed records within a relative 1% tolerance (accepted number > 20,000 per step). All Monte Carlo simulations and data analyses were performed in R (v4.3.1), and the code is provided in the Code Availability section. Uncertainties in accepted solutions for each flux are shown as 68% and 95% confidence intervals in Fig. 2. Since modeled FHT and FLT are nearly identical at each step and highly correlated over the Phanerozoic (R² = 0.84; Supplementary Figs. 2−3), they are combined as a total Mg-silicate sink (Fsil; Fig. 2c) in subsequent discussions.

Our inverse model avoids reliance on fragmentary sedimentary records or uncertain tectonic reconstructions and enables the simultaneous quantification of the major Mg fluxes into and out of ocean water over the Phanerozoic. Moreover, by including the variation of seawater [Mg] in Eq. (1), our model explicitly incorporates temporal variations in Mg residence time. To test the robustness of our results, we performed local sensitivity tests in which each input variable was varied within its data-driven uncertainty and the resulting ensembles were evaluated using Partial Rank Correlation Coefficients (PRCC) and local Δrange effect sizes to quantify short-term, monotonic controls on each flux. These local tests capture how small, realistic deviations in seawater [Mg], δ²⁶MgSW, Δdol-SW, ΔLT-SW, δ²⁶Mgriv, and prior input ranges propagate into Friv, Fdol, and Fsil at each time step (see Methods for details). For the secular analysis, we first calculated time-step mean fluxes and then aggregated them into 20-Myr bins, relating the binned mean fluxes to the slowly varying boundary conditions, including seawater [Mg], δ²⁶MgSW, Δdol-SW, and δ²⁶Mgriv, using a Deming regression that accounts for uncertainties in both variables.

Our sensitivity tests show that, for the integrated time step flux variations, the directions of flux changes are primarily governed by δ²⁶MgSW whereas their magnitudes are mainly controlled by seawater [Mg], with the prescribed Friv range additionally modulating its own variability (Fig. 3; Supplementary Figs. 4–9). Over the whole Phanerozoic, δ²⁶MgSW continues to dictate the direction of dolomite and riverine flux, while seawater [Mg] mainly determines the direction of Fsil. Variations in dolomite and riverine fluxes are mainly controlled by δ²⁶MgSW, while Fsil variation is dominated by seawater [Mg] (Fig. 4). We additionally explored scenarios in which the FLT is higher than the FHT (FLT = 1–3 Tmol/yr and FHT = 0.6–2.5 Tmol/yr). The resulting solutions are indistinguishable from our primary outputs (Supplementary Fig. 10), demonstrating that the assumption of a higher FHT relative to FLT does not influence our results. Together, these analyses demonstrate that the inferred controls on all Mg fluxes arise predominantly from the intrinsic mass-balance framework and from seawater [Mg] and δ²⁶MgSW variations, rather than from prior ranges of input-flux or isotope-fractionation factors.

Major drivers of phanerozoic seawater Mg/Ca variation
The Phanerozoic evolution of seawater [Mg] can be divided into six stages according to our fitted curve, comprising two full cycles of decreasing, fluctuating (minor variation), and increasing seawater [Mg] (Fig. 2a). Seawater [Mg] decreased from 550 to 500 Ma, remained relatively stable with minor fluctuations between 500 and 390 Ma, and increased from 390 to 310 Ma. The second cycle began with a decline in seawater [Mg] from 310 to 200 Ma, followed by a fluctuating interval between 200 and 90 Ma, and a final increase from 90 to 0 Ma. These intervals closely parallel secular variations in seawater Mg/Ca and the timing of aragonite–calcite transitions (Fig. 2a). In our model, we force source-sink net Mg imbalance (Fluxsource-sink) to co-vary with seawater [Mg] to maintain mass balance, ensuring positive Fluxsource-sink values during seawater [Mg] increase periods (Fig. 2e). Over the Phanerozoic, average Mg flux ranges are 5.2–5.4 Tmol/yr for Friv, 1.4–2.8 Tmol/yr for Fdol, and 2.9–3.9 Tmol/yr for Fsil (Fig. 2b–e).

Seawater [Mg] varies in concert with seawater Mg/Ca throughout the Phanerozoic, and the same geological drivers that regulate seawater [Mg] also control seawater Mg/Ca. Seawater [Mg] and [Ca] are independently reconstructed by measuring Mg and Ca concentrations of fluid inclusions in early-stage primary marine halite23, and their inverse evolution, together with the co-variation of seawater [Mg] and Mg/Ca (Fig. 1a–b), suggests that these secular variations are driven by the same geological processes. During intervals of decreasing and increasing seawater [Mg], seawater [Mg] and Mg/Ca show strong positive correlations (R² = 0.93–0.99; Supplementary Fig. 11), indicating that processes responsible for [Mg] changes also regulate Ca and the Mg/Ca ratio. This is reasonable since two major geological processes, seafloor alteration and dolomitization, involve 1:1 Mg-Ca exchange, such that seawater [Mg] increases correspond to [Ca] decreases and vice versa. In contrast, during intervals of minor seawater [Mg] fluctuations, correlations between [Mg] and Mg/Ca weaken (R² = 0.01–0.53; Supplementary Fig. 11) while seawater [Ca] varied significantly (Fig. 1b). This indicates that independent Ca-related processes, such as calcium carbonate burial, also considerably regulate seawater Mg/Ca during these periods. For instance, the development of pelagic calcification since the Mesozoic may have significantly contributed to declining seawater [Ca]24. In the following sections, we focus on the primary controls on major seawater Mg/Ca transitions between aragonite and calcite seas, while secondary fluctuations within prolonged calcite-sea intervals (ca. 500–390 and 200–90 Ma) may be better constrained through future studies of the marine Ca cycle.

The limited Friv variation in our results does not suggest invariant Friv in the geological record; instead, it reflects the relative insensitivity of Mg mass balance to Friv within plausible ranges. The modest Friv increases during the 420–370 Ma and 50–0 Ma periods coincide with the assembly of the supercontinent Pangea and Alpine-Himalayan collision (Fig. 2b), suggesting enhanced weathering flux during supercontinent assembly. The increase in Friv during 550–500 Ma may reflect intensified weathering and a reorganized clay factory associated with widespread felsic terrains, high continental topography, and elevated CO₂ outgassing14,25–27. However, our model cannot resolve the precise magnitude of these variations. This insensitivity does not substantially affect our interpretation because weathering generally alters Mg and Ca inputs in the same direction unless global lithology changes substantially, and the Phanerozoic continental lithologic composition appears to have remained broadly stable28. Nevertheless, short-lived shifts in lithology can influence riverine Mg/Ca, because calcium carbonate (Mg/Ca ≈ 0.1)4, dolomite (Mg/Ca = 1.0)29, and silicate rocks (Mg/Ca ≈ 0.4 to 0.7)30 contribute distinct Mg/Ca signatures. For instance, the extensive exposure of basalt-mafic rocks during the formation of Pangea at the late Permian31, the enhanced development of carbonate platforms during the breakup of Pangea at the Jurassic-Cretaceous32, and the Alpine-Himalayan Collision during the Cenozoic mountain uplift33 may involve significant changes in global continental lithology. Improved constraints on continental weathering fluxes and lithologic evolution across these intervals would further refine estimates of riverine Mg delivery and Mg/Ca modulation.

Finally, Phanerozoic seawater Mg/Ca variations can be primarily attributed to substantial changes in dolomite and Mg-silicate fluxes. Between 550 and 500 Ma, intense Mg-silicate removal coincided with net Mg loss (e.g., negative Fluxsource-sink), leading to a decline in seawater Mg/Ca, while subsequent weakening of this sink mitigated this decline; the dolomite sink remained nearly constant (Fig. 2). From 500 to 390 Ma, a slight decrease in Fdol combined with an initial rise and subsequent fall in Fsil yielded slightly positive and later negative Fluxsource-sink, accounting for fluctuating seawater Mg/Ca within this prolonged calcite sea period (Fig. 2a–d). Between 390 and 310 Ma, rising seawater Mg/Ca was first driven by a sharp reduction in the dolomite sink (390–340 Ma), followed by weakening of the Mg-silicate sink at 340–310 Ma (Fig. 2a–d). From 310 to 200 Ma, concurrent peaks in both dolomite and Mg-silicate fluxes caused renewed Mg removal and a further decline in Mg/Ca. Despite decreases in both sinks after 240 Ma, Fluxsource-sink remained negative, sustaining the downward trend (Fig. 2a–d). During 200–90 Ma, reduced dolomitization was offset by enhanced Mg-silicate removal, maintaining fluctuating seawater Mg/Ca (Fig. 2a–d). Since 90 Ma, rising seawater [Mg] was driven by a persistent decline in the dolomite sink, amplified after 40 Ma by weakening Mg-silicate removal (Fig. 2a–d).

Controls on Mg-silicate and dolomite fluxes
Marine Mg-silicate formation is considered to be dominated by seawater–seafloor reactions, with clay authigenesis contributing negligibly under Phanerozoic conditions of low dissolved silica and cooler bottom-water temperatures34. For instance, the modern ocean hosts an authigenic clay sink of only 0.02 Tmol/yr5, representing ~0.6% of the total Mg-silicate sink. Mg-silicate flux during seafloor alteration is mainly controlled by seafloor spreading, with faster spreading rates producing more fresh ocean crust available for hydrothermal alteration and Mg-silicate formation7. The tight correlation between FHT and FLT further supports a dominant driver of seafloor spreading on both fluxes (Supplementary Figs. 2–3), with the authigenic clay sink playing only a minor role.

Mg-silicate flux exhibits five prominent peaks at ca. 550, 420, 335, 240, and 110–40 Ma (Fig. 2c). Four of five peaks lag the corresponding maxima in reconstructed global seafloor production rate by 10–30 Myr, consistent with the observation that most hydrothermal alteration of oceanic crust occurs within 30 Myr of crustal accretion6,35. The exception at ca. 420 Ma, which lags the production maximum by ~50 Myr (Fig. 2c), may reflect uncertainties in fluid-inclusion [Mg] data and/or prolonged seafloor–seawater reactions, which can persist for up to 80 Myr35. Notably, the protracted Mg-silicate flux between ~140 and 40 Ma closely matches previously reconstructed hydrothermal fluxes during Pangea dispersal (140–35 Ma; Fig. 2f–g)36. Moreover, Fsil is negatively correlated with the continental fragmentation index during Pangea early assembly (500–320 Ma) and positively correlated during dispersal (200–0 Ma; Fig. 2c, g; Supplementary Fig. 12). These relationships indicate that Mg-silicate formation was significantly enhanced during active tectonic phases (assembly and breakup), whereas it was attenuated during periods of supercontinent stasis. These relationships highlight a strong coupling between the supercontinent cycle, seafloor production, and marine Mg-silicate formation.

Controls on dolomitization rate remain unclear. High sea level29, warm climates13,37, large-scale restriction38, the dissolution-reprecipitation process39, oceanic anoxia40, and microbial activity41 have all been proposed to promote dolomite formation. Microbial activity, elevated temperatures, and restricted hydrological conditions are suggested to accelerate dolomite nucleation and crystal growth37,39,41, while anoxic conditions can further stimulate microbial metabolisms that catalyze dolomitization. High sea level promotes expansive shallow platforms and accelerates reaction kinetics through enhanced evaporation and elevated temperatures, particularly in warm, semi-restricted settings29. Sea level and climate are fundamentally modulated by tectonics: supercontinent assembly leads to a lower sea level due to thermal contraction of aging seafloor and crustal thickening during continental collision, whereas breakup creates younger seafloor and thinner crust, raising sea level42,43. Warm climates typically accompany early supercontinent breakup, when diminished continental collision reduces silicate weathering, and increased arc volcanism, mantle plumes, and large igneous provinces drive rapid pCO₂ increases26,44,45. Large-scale restriction is controlled by global tectonic configuration46, while oceanic anoxia and microbial activity are influenced by atmospheric O₂ and broader environmental conditions, which have also been linked to the supercontinent cycle47,48.

Dolomite abundance has been reconstructed using various approaches, providing an independent benchmark for comparison with our dolomite flux evolution. Our modeled dolomite flux reproduces the major features of sedimentary records, including high dolomite abundance in the early Paleozoic and across the Permian–Triassic boundary, reduced values during the Mississippian, and a long-term decline since the early Mesozoic (Fig. 2d, 5)29,40. We further standardized all dolomite abundance curves through age alignment and long-term trend extraction using Generalized Additive Models and Locally Estimated Scatterplot Smoothing, to directly compare dolomite flux with those dolomite abundance curves. Spearman’s rank correlations (ρ) and bootstrap resampling of the aligned trends show strong agreement between our dolomite flux and three of the five sedimentary records (Fig. 5, Supplementary Fig. 13; ρ > 0.67). The remaining two records show weaker agreement due to intrinsic limitations, one with extremely low temporal resolution, and the other exhibiting a temporal pattern distinct from the broader dataset (Fig. 5).

Correlations between dolomite flux and environmental factors suggest that the dominant controls on dolomitization varied over the Phanerozoic. Dolomite flux is generally high in the early Paleozoic and declines through the Mesozoic, mirroring the secular evolution of atmospheric pO₂ (Fig. 5), suggesting a potential role of oceanic anoxia and microbial mediation on secular dolomite formation. Moreover, dolomite flux shows strong positive correlations with modeled pCO₂ (550–340 and 250–0 Ma) and reconstructed sea level (460–340 and 100–0 Ma) during most Phanerozoic intervals (Fig. 5, Supplementary Fig. 11), consistent with dominant control of climatic and eustatic variations on dolomite formation. However, the pronounced rise in dolomite flux between 340 and 250 Ma coincides with a low pCO₂ and low sea level interval (Fig. 5), suggesting other factors also influence dolomitization. This elevated dolomite flux may be attributed to the restriction of the Paleotethys Ocean during Pangea assembly38, which is also favored by arid continental climates and widespread evaporite deposition46 during this period.

The role of Phanerozoic supercontinent cycles on seawater Mg/Ca
Previous studies have emphasized the influence of tectonics and climate on Phanerozoic seawater Mg/Ca8,36,49, yet direct constraints on how these processes modulated marine Mg fluxes have been lacking. Our model quantitatively constrains variations in Mg-silicate and dolomite fluxes and reveals their tight links to specific tectonic–climatic processes (Fig. 2). Across the Phanerozoic, high Mg/Ca ratios broadly coincide with low sea level and coolhouse conditions associated with supercontinent assembly and major collisional phases, whereas low Mg/Ca ratios correspond to high sea level and greenhouse climates during supercontinent dispersal (Fig. 2). Our results show that this inverse relationship between seawater Mg/Ca and sea level reflects the combined impact of tectonics and climate on Mg-silicate formation and dolomitization. Collectively, these findings imply that the supercontinent cycle exerted a first-order control on Phanerozoic seawater Mg/Ca.

The supercontinent cycle regulates Phanerozoic seawater Mg/Ca as follows: during supercontinent early assembly (e.g. Pangea) or major collisional events (e.g. Cenozoic Alpine-Himalayan collisions), attenuated seafloor spreading and cooler climates suppress Mg-silicate formation and dolomitization, thereby increasing seawater Mg/Ca and shifting global oceans from calcite to aragonite seas (Fig. 6a). During periods of supercontinent early breakup, enhanced seafloor spreading and warmer climates stimulate both Mg-silicate formation and dolomitization, lowering Mg/Ca and returning the oceans to calcite seas (Fig. 6b). During intervals of stable supercontinent dispersal or sluggish plate reorganization, both tectonic and climatic conditions remain relatively steady, yielding limited variability in Mg fluxes and sustaining prolonged calcite seas (Fig. 6c). The supercontinent cycle also drives long-term variations in calcium carbonate deposition by modulating global shelf area50. Supercontinent breakup expands flooded margins and enhances CaCO₃ burial, whereas assembly contracts shelf space and suppresses CaCO₃ deposition. Because this process consumes more Ca during breakup and dispersal but significantly less during assembly, and contributes only marginally to the marine Mg cycle, its influence on Phanerozoic seawater Mg/Ca is likely important only during seawater [Mg] fluctuation periods (Fig. 2a).

Beyond Mg/Ca, the supercontinent cycle has been invoked to regulate other major and trace elements in seawater. Phanerozoic seawater sulfate shows a broadly similar evolution to Mg, which potentially reflects enhanced removal during high-sea-level intervals when microbial sulfate reduction8 and Ca-driven sulfate precipitation intensified49. Seawater Sr and Li concentrations also appear tied to the supercontinent cycle, decreasing during assembly and rising during breakup and dispersal, likely due to their sensitivity to changes in hydrothermal fluid fluxes51,52. These trace elements, strongly modulated by hydrothermal activity51,52, are therefore particularly responsive to tectonic reorganization associated with supercontinent cycling.

By integrating elemental and isotopic records into a marine Mg-cycle model, our study provides quantitative estimates of long-term fluxes through the major Mg sinks in seawater. This advance allows seawater Mg/Ca variability to be more directly attributed to specific geological processes. Our results offer a framework for interpreting Phanerozoic seawater chemistry variations and demonstrate that these variations reflect coupled interactions among ocean chemistry, sedimentation, climate, and the supercontinent cycle.

---

## Methods

Model inputs
Required parameters in our model include Δdol-SW, ΔHT-SW, ΔLT-SW, and input ranges of Friv, FHT, FLT, and Fdol. Temperature-dependent Δdol-SW has been experimentally constrained20: Δdol-SW = -0.1554(±0.0096) × 10⁶/T². Calculated Δdol-SW is -1.8 ± 0.1‰ at 20 °C. Considering the variation of Earth’s surface temperature from ~9 to ~33 °C in the Phanerozoic21, we allow Δdol-SW to vary with temperature and propagate uncertainty in the equation (from -1.95 ± 0.1‰ to -1.66 ± 0.1‰). During high-temperature seafloor-seawater reactions, Mg is removed quantitatively from fluid to crust with nil isotope fractionation6,16, and we therefore set ΔHT-SW to 0‰. During low-temperature Mg-silicate formation, previous studies consistently suggest a positive ΔLT-SW, varying from 0.1‰ to 1.1‰ in authigenic clays5, with average values of 0.8‰ to 1‰ in altered oceanic crust17,18, and 0.25‰ to 7‰ in hydrothermal fluids19. Most studies adopt 0.6–0.8‰, and we therefore set 0.8 ± 0.2‰ to encompass a relatively large range in previous constraints. Reference ranges of these isotope fractionation in previous studies and this study are summarized in Supplementary Table 1.

Ranges of Friv, FHT, FLT, and Fdol for the implementation of Monte Carlo simulations in our model are grounded in previous estimates on modern and Phanerozoic models. Previous estimates on Friv, FHT, FLT, and Fdol range from 4 to 6.1 Tmol/yr, 0.24 to 2.6 Tmol/yr, 0.6 to 2.5 Tmol/yr, and 0.75 to 3 Tmol/yr, and we set a range of 4.5–6 Tmol/yr, 1–3 Tmol/yr, 0.6–2.5 Tmol/yr, and 1–4 Tmol/yr for input ranges of Friv, FHT, FLT, and Fdol in our model (Supplementary Table 2). Since some studies suggest lower FHT than that of FLT19, we also considered a scenario using ranges of 1–3 Tmol/yr for FLT and 0.6–2.5 Tmol/yr for FHT, which resulted in identical results to our primary outputs (Supplementary Fig. 10). To verify whether these inputs can effectively cover the actual ranges of these fluxes over the whole Phanerozoic and whether these prior input ranges would affect our model outputs, we further included variable upper and lower ranges for these fluxes at each time step to quantify their effect on our results in the following sensitivity tests.

Sensitivity test
We evaluate two types of controls on the modeled riverine, Mg-silicate, and dolomite Mg fluxes: (1) local sensitivity at each individual time step, and (2) secular drivers across the Phanerozoic. The local sensitivity quantifies which parameters constrain flux magnitudes within a given time step, whereas the secular analysis identifies which boundary conditions primarily explain the long-term evolution of these fluxes through Earth’s history. For both analyses, we use Partial Rank Correlation Coefficients (PRCC) to quantify the independent (partial) monotonic control of each variable on each flux, and we use Δrange metrics (ΔY or ΔF) to quantify the corresponding amplitude of that control in physical units (Tmol/yr).

Monte Carlo sampling was used to identify flux combinations satisfying mass–isotope balance, whereas Latin Hypercube Sampling was employed to systematically explore parameter sensitivities around these solutions. For each time step, we generated 3×10⁴ Latin Hypercube samples (LHS) covering the full range of model parameters. LHS provides uniform, stratified coverage of the parameter space, enabling efficient yet comprehensive exploration of model behavior. Local perturbations follow the data-driven uncertainties: seawater [Mg] is drawn from 68% confidence bounds, and δ²⁶MgSW is perturbed by ± 0.2‰, which is derived from current uncertainty in the reconstructed Phanerozoic curve13. Δdol–SW is drawn via the temperature-dependent coefficient (0.1554 ± 0.0096) × 10⁶/T², ΔLT–SW is sampled in 0.6–1.0‰, and δ²⁶Mgriv in ± 0.1‰. Physically plausible Mg fluxes are allowed by first drawing a lower and upper bound for each flux in Tmol/yr, then sampling uniformly within that interval: Friv is allowed to vary between ~4.5 and 6.0 Tmol/yr (Friv_min = 4.5–5.0; Friv_max = 5.5–6.0), Fdol between ~1 and 4 Tmol/yr (Fdol_min = 1.0–1.5; Fdol_max = 3.5–4.0), FHT between 1 and 3 Tmol/yr (FHT_min = 1.0–1.5; FHT_max = 2.5–3.0), and FLT between 0.6 and 2.5 Tmol/yr (FLT_min = 0.6–1.2; FLT_max = 2.0–2.5). These accepted ensembles form the foundation for both the local and secular analyses, while parameters that exhibit genuine secular trends are evaluated in the secular framework. Local sensitivity therefore reflects uncertainty within each geological interval, whereas the secular analysis evaluates the effect of boundary-condition evolution through time.

(a) Partial Rank Correlation Coefficients (PRCC)
PRCC quantifies the monotonic influence of each parameter (Xᵢ) on a modeled flux (Y) while removing covariation with all other parameters. For the local analysis, at each time step, all variables are rank-transformed, Xᵢ and Y are separately regressed against all remaining parameters, and the Spearman correlation (ρ) between their residuals defines the local PRCC:

PRCC(Xᵢ, Y) = ρ(rXi, rY) (3)

The sign indicates whether Xᵢ increases or decreases Y, and |PRCC| measures the strength of that relationship. |PRCC| values are interpreted following common practice, with higher absolute values indicating stronger monotonic influence. Local PRCCs reveal, for each time step, which parameters co-vary with the flux to satisfy Mg mass–isotope balance. For each time step, we additionally apply a nonparametric bootstrap by resampling the accepted Monte Carlo ensembles with replacement (1000 iterations) and recalculating PRCC, yielding a bootstrap distribution for that interval. The bootstrap median provides a stable PRCC estimate for that specific time step. We then integrate all local PRCC results across ~550 time steps to compute the median and interquartile range (IQR) for each parameter–flux pair.

(b) Effect size (Δrange).
To complement the correlation-based PRCC, we compute the physical amplitude of each parameter’s effect using Δrange metrics. In the local analysis, all accepted ensembles within a given time step are sorted by parameter X and divided into quantile bins; the difference between median fluxes in the highest and lowest bins define the local effect size (ΔY):

ΔY = median(Y|Xhigh) - median(Y|Xlow) (4)

ΔY (in Tmol/yr) represents the characteristic amplitude by which that parameter can shift the flux within that specific interval. Within each time step, ΔY is also bootstrapped by resampling accepted ensembles and recalculating ΔY 1000 times, producing a bootstrap ΔY distribution whose median represents the interval-specific effect size. Local ΔY values are likewise summarized across ~550 time steps (median ± IQR), where the reported 550 Ma statistics are derived from the set of per-interval bootstrap medians, reflecting long-term variability in effect magnitude.

(c) Secular drivers (20 Myr binned Deming regression with bootstrap)
To evaluate the leverage of boundary conditions on long-term flux evolution over the Phanerozoic, time-series data were aggregated into 20 Myr bins, and binned mean fluxes (F: Friv, Fsil, Fdol) were related to binned boundary conditions (X: seawater [Mg], δ²⁶MgSW, δ²⁶Mgriv, Δdol–SW). We first applied a Deming (total least-squares) regression, which accounts for uncertainties in both X and F, to estimate the secular slope:

F = a + bX, b = dF/dX (5)

ΔF = b × (Xmax - Xmin) (6)

Where b is the long-term Deming slope (dF/dX), ΔF is the flux change implied by the secular range of X, and the coefficient of determination (R²) is computed from fitted versus observed fluxes to evaluate explanatory power. The secular analysis is limited to parameters that exhibit genuine secular trends and can therefore drive multi-million-year flux evolution, whereas time-invariant parameters such as ΔLT-SW or prior ranges only affect local solutions and are not evaluated in the secular framework. We then apply a nonparametric bootstrap that resamples the 20 Myr bins with replacement (N≈27 per iteration), recalculating the Deming slope and ΔF for each realization. The resulting bootstrap medians and IQRs quantify the robustness of long-term relationships to temporal sampling.

The combined framework thus links instantaneous and long-term controls: local PRCC and ΔY capture short-term parameter sensitivity within each interval, their time-integrated medians reveal persistent controls across the Phanerozoic, and the secular regression (ΔF and R²) quantifies the actual magnitude and explanatory power of slow boundary-condition variations.
